guide: V35 labeling guide + V36 addendum (adversarial categories); each author saw only a catalog of grounded source sentences
note: V36 sealed split: four independent annotators (F, G, H, I) writing in four voices, written after the V36 reader was frozen, scored once. Aggregates only.

cases.text: Function plus its enclosing scope.
credits: function together with access to its
cases.notes: Only five words, but 'function plus its enclosing scope' is the whole definition (a function together with access to its surrounding lexical environment) and nothing is wrong.
cases.author: F

cases.text: A load balancer operates rather like a clearing house: each incoming request is allocated to one of several interchangeable copies of the backend, and any copy that fails its health check is simply left out of the allocation.
credits: distributes incoming traffic across multiple healthy backend
cases.notes: Spreading requests over healthy backend copies is right, but the purpose (scalability, availability, failover) is never stated, so mostlyUnderstood rather than understood.
cases.author: F

cases.text: Time complexity measures how the amount of work scales as the input grows, relative to whatever cost model has been assumed. A linear scan necessarily examines every single element, there is no way round that, whereas binary search works by putting the data into order as it goes, halving the range at each step.

misconceptions.claim: linear scan may inspect every element
the data must have a compatible ordering

credits: how work grows with input size
cases.notes: Growth of work with input under a model is right, but 'necessarily examines every single element' makes the source's 'may' absolute, and binary search is said to produce the ordering that the source makes its precondition.
cases.author: F

cases.text: Structured output is to a language model what a standardised form is to a bureaucracy: instead of free prose the model must answer by filling in fixed fields, some of which accept only values from a set list, so that the program downstream can parse the answer reliably and check it against the schema before relying on it.
credits: machine-readable schema such as JSON fields/enums
AI output safer to consume programmatically
cases.notes: Constraining the model's answer to fixed fields and allowed values, and the resulting safe programmatic consumption with schema checks, are both expressed correctly through a bureaucratic-form analogy.
cases.author: F

cases.text: I think a pattern is kind of about design problems that keep coming back? like something to do with recurring problems, maybe.
cases.notes: Ties patterns to recurring design problems but never says when a pattern is useful (when it makes the problem easier to understand): the right words without the relationship.
cases.author: F

cases.text: One should hand the screens a small immutable summary of the document rather than the database object itself; the justification is essentially one of transaction costs, since database objects are heavy and shipping them through every screen consumes memory and slows down each render.
cases.notes: The design choice (an immutable summary instead of the database object) is right, but it is justified by memory and speed, whereas the source's reason is keeping boundaries changeable and rendering separate from storage details.
cases.author: F

cases.text: React and the screen.
cases.notes: Four words naming React and the screen; nothing about rendering calculating the UI description, so there is nothing to judge.
cases.author: F

cases.text: TypeScript is, in essence, JavaScript to which a static type system has been added, the types being checked before the program is ever run, so that a good many integration mistakes are caught early; the annotations double as documentation of the contracts between modules, for colleagues and editor tooling alike. Compatibility is decided by shape rather than by name, much as an enzyme accepts any substrate that fits its active site. Quite often the type need not be written at all, since the compiler works it out from the value, and it also validates network data at runtime, so a malformed API response is rejected on arrival.

misconceptions.claim: does not validate network data at runtime

credits: static type system checked before runtime
catches many integration mistakes earlier and documents
can often determine a value's type
cases.notes: Everything (static types checked before runtime, early error catching, contracts, structural compatibility, inference) is right except the one clause that TypeScript validates network data at runtime, which the source explicitly denies.
cases.author: F

cases.text: The rule is quite simple: never use the array index as a key, under any circumstances, because it is always wrong. The safest choice is to generate a fresh random key on every render, since a brand-new key guarantees that React treats each item as up to date.

misconceptions.claim: array index can be a poor key
random key also destroys continuity between renders

cases.notes: Turns 'an index can be a poor key when items move, are inserted or removed' into an absolute ban and recommends fresh random keys per render, which the source says destroy continuity between renders.
cases.author: F

cases.text: For instance, when my browser keeps the department logo after the first visit so that it doesn't have to download it all over again every time I open a page.
cases.notes: A single browser example of reusing a stored copy, with no general statement of a faster layer keeping reusable results or of its benefits and risks; torn with mostlyUnderstood, chose fragile because the idea never leaves the example.
cases.author: F

cases.text: As I understand it, a closure is not the function on its own but the function taken together with the environment in which it was written: from inside the function one can still reach the variables that were in scope around it. The analogy I find most helpful is that of a symbiont, which cannot really be described apart from the host it lives in and continues to draw upon; the function, similarly, keeps drawing on its surroundings.
credits: function together with access to its
cases.notes: A function paired with continuing access to the variables around where it was written is the full definition, given here with a symbiont analogy; nothing is wrong.
cases.author: F

cases.text: Context does not spare you the intermediate components: the value is still handed down by hand through every layer until it reaches the descendant that needs it, much like goods moving along a supply chain in which each middleman must take possession before passing them on. For that reason it is best reserved for data that only one component cares about, rather than app-wide matters such as the theme or the logged-in user.

misconceptions.claim: without manually passing it through every
fits cross-cutting data such as theme

cases.notes: Describes prop drilling (passing the value by hand through every intermediate component), which is exactly what the source says Context avoids, and then denies that it suits cross-cutting data such as theme or the authenticated user.
cases.author: F

cases.text: it's how work grows with input size (under some model). linear search always ends up touching every item, and binary search sorts the list while it narrows it down

misconceptions.claim: linear scan may inspect every element
the data must have a compatible ordering

credits: how work grows with input size
cases.notes: Same understanding as the group: growth with input size is right, 'always ends up touching every item' overgeneralizes the qualified 'may', and binary search is said to sort the data it actually requires to be ordered.
cases.author: F

cases.text: Splits incoming requests among several working server copies.
credits: distributes incoming traffic across multiple healthy backend
cases.notes: Requests shared among healthy ('working') instances is the definition, but nothing says why (scalability, availability, failover), as in the rest of the group.
cases.author: F

cases.text: An abstraction is a simplified model that hides whatever detail doesn't matter for the task in hand, much as a price summarises an entire supply chain for the buyer, who has no need to know about the farms and freighters behind it. It lets whoever uses it think at the appropriate level, and ideally it conceals the parts most likely to change while exposing what the consumer actually cares about.
credits: hides irrelevant detail for a particular task
lets callers reason at the right level
cases.notes: A simplified model hiding task-irrelevant detail, the right-level purpose and hiding volatility are all expressed correctly through a price analogy.
cases.author: F

cases.text: As far as I can tell, the notion of a pattern is bound up with the recurrence of design problems, the same kind of difficulty presenting itself again and again across different systems.
cases.notes: Links patterns to recurring design problems but gives no account of when a pattern is useful (making the problem easier to understand), so the central relationship is missing.
cases.author: F

cases.text: It's when it does its thing so it shows up.
cases.notes: The repeated 'it' leaves unclear what acts on what, and 'shows up' says nothing about calculating a description; as empty as the rest of the group.
cases.author: F

cases.text: Give screens an immutable summary, not the DB object, because the DB object's too heavy and makes the UI slow.
cases.notes: Right recommendation (immutable summary, not the database object) justified by weight and speed, which the source does not give; its reason is changeable boundaries and keeping rendering separate from storage.
cases.author: F

cases.text: Continous integration refers to the automatic merging of changes through a repeatable battery of checks: build, lint, type checking, tests. It is often asserted that CI catches defects, but strictly speaking what one observes is a correlation; teams which use CI tend to ship fewer defects, which may simply reflect that better-run teams adopt it, not that the checks themselves stop anything before the merge.

misconceptions.claim: It catches defects before merge

credits: automatically integrating changes through repeatable checks
cases.notes: The definition is right, but the source's causal claim that CI catches defects before merge is recast as a mere correlation explained by team quality.
cases.author: F

cases.text: It's like a library: the actual files are kept under a stable ID, and alongside them there's a separate catalogue of metadata that people can search through.
credits: original files by stable identifier
cases.notes: Retells the library example correctly but never states the lesson (different representations serve different operations; choose by the operations that must be cheap, not by sophistication), so the central idea is only implied.
cases.author: F

cases.text: Primitive values are simply the basic built-in objects of JavaScript: strings, numbers, booleans, arrays and the like. When one of them is assigned to a second variable, both names end up pointing at one and the same value, so that if b is later changed, a changes along with it; that, surely, is the whole point of calling them primitive.

misconceptions.claim: JavaScript values that are not objects
Assigning them copies the value

cases.notes: Calls primitives objects (even listing arrays) and gives them shared-reference assignment, the object behaviour the source contrasts them with; two distinct errors.
cases.author: F

cases.text: Put simply, a closure is when the outer function holds on to the variables of the inner function, so that the enclosing function can still reach whatever was declared inside the nested one.

misconceptions.claim: access to its surrounding lexical environment

cases.notes: Reverses the direction of access: the function keeps access to its surrounding (outer) environment, not the outer function to the inner function's variables.
cases.author: F

cases.text: An enviroment variable is, so to speak, a labelled setting (a name paired with a value) which the running process picks up from the environment it has been launched in; the address of the database, or a flag saying whether this is production, would be typical instances.
credits: configuration value provided by the process environment
cases.notes: The definition (a key-value setting supplied by the process environment) is right, but the reason it matters, keeping deploy-time configuration out of source code, is not stated.
cases.author: F

cases.text: Section one follows a browser request on its round trip: how it travels over the network, how routing and load balancers direct it to the right server, where a cache or CDN may answer it early, and how the response makes its way back, rather as one might trace a shipment through a distribution network of hubs and regional warehouses.
credits: How browser requests travel, get routed
cases.notes: Travel, routing, caching and return of browser requests are all covered in different words, naming routing, load balancing and caching along the way; nothing is wrong.
cases.author: F

cases.text: In binary search the ordering of the collection is brought about by the repeated bisection itself, whereas in a linear scan each and every element is invariably inspected; what time complexity captures, under a chosen model of cost, is the rate at which work increases with the size of the input, rather like a dose-response curve.

misconceptions.claim: linear scan may inspect every element
the data must have a compatible ordering

credits: how work grows with input size
cases.notes: Same two errors as the group in passive, reordered form: every element 'invariably' inspected overgeneralizes 'may', and bisection is said to create the ordering that binary search presupposes.
cases.author: F

cases.text: Patterns have to do with recurring design problems.
cases.notes: Names the recurring design problem but not what makes a pattern useful (easier understanding); a gesture at the idea rather than the relationship.
cases.author: F

cases.text: Incoming traffic is apportioned by the balancer among multiple instances of the backend, rather as an ant colony divides foraging among its workers, with any instance judged unhealthy being withdrawn from the rotation.
credits: distributes incoming traffic across multiple healthy backend
cases.notes: Distribution over healthy instances is stated in passive, biological terms; the purpose (scalability, availability, failover) is absent, as in the rest of the group.
cases.author: F

cases.text: Rendering is, if I have understood the notes correctly, one of the keystone processes of the React ecosystem, in much the way that metabolism is one of the fundamental processes of a living organism: a great deal of the framework's behaviour is organised around it, it has to do with what the user ends up seeing on the screen, and it is therefore clearly something that anyone working on interfaces ought to understand well.
cases.notes: Long and fluent but content-free: rendering is 'fundamental' and concerns what appears on screen, with no statement that it calculates the UI description.
cases.author: F

cases.text: Just as a cell exports a compact signalling molecule rather than the organelle that made it, the application should pass the view an immutable summary instead of the database object; this is favoured chiefly because the full object is metabolically expensive, being large in memory and slow to re-render.
cases.notes: Right choice (an immutable summary rather than the database object) defended on memory and re-render cost, a reason the source never gives; it cites changeable boundaries and separating rendering from storage.
cases.author: F

cases.text: By 'closure' is meant the pairing of a function with its lexical surroundings, such that the variables visible at the point where the function was defined remain reachable from within its body.
credits: function together with access to its
cases.notes: A function paired with reachable variables from where it was defined is exactly a function with access to its surrounding lexical environment; correct and complete.
cases.author: F

cases.text: It lets it change straight away on the screen, then it gets compared with the one the server has, and if they don't match it has to be sorted out somehow.
cases.notes: Gestures at an immediate local change followed by reconciliation with the server, but the pronouns hide what changes and what is compared, and version/conflict rules and the purpose are missing; torn with mostlyUnderstood, chose fragile.
cases.author: F

cases.text: TypeScript = JavaScript plus types that get checked before the code actually runs. You often don't even have to write the types, it works them out from the values. None of that survives at runtime though, transpilation strips it all back to plain JS.
credits: static type system checked before runtime
can often determine a value's type
cases.notes: Definition, (often) inferred types and erasure at runtime are right, but the purpose (catching integration mistakes early and documenting contracts) is missing.
cases.author: F

cases.text: I would describe a cache in terms of inventory: rather than manufacturing every order from raw materials, a shop keeps finished goods on a shelf near the till, so repeat requests are served quickly and the factory (the database, or a paid API) is spared the expensive work. The gains are lower latency, less database load, lower API bills and less computation. The price is freshness, since the shelf may hold yesterday's goods, plus extra complexity; and, somewhat counter-intuitively, if the shelf empties at a bad moment every customer is sent to the factory at once, so load can spike exactly when protection was most needed.
credits: faster storage layer that keeps reusable results
can reduce latency, database load, API cost
can accidentally amplify load exactly when
cases.notes: A faster store of reusable results, the latency/load/cost gains, the freshness trade-off and the load-amplification risk are all correct, through an inventory analogy.
cases.author: F

cases.text: Keys work rather like the ear tags a field biologist attaches to animals: they let React recognise each list item as the same individual from one render to the next, so that when the list is reshuffled no item ends up with another item's local state. Using the item's position in the array as its tag is risky, since positions change whenever items move, are added or are taken out.
credits: stable key helps React match an item
should not make one item inherit
array index can be a poor key
cases.notes: Identity matching across renders, no inheriting of another item's state and the index risk are right, but the point that a freshly generated random key destroys continuity is missing.
cases.author: F

cases.text: Infinite feeds are a textbook case of the attention economy: platforms build endless scrolling because it maximises engagement and therefore advertising revenue, and there is some evidence that it encourages compulsive use.
cases.notes: True-sounding remarks on the economics of engagement, but nothing about the drill's scenario (millions of rows, continuous scrolling, new rows being inserted).
cases.author: F

cases.text: Hash tables give constant-time lookups on average, balanced search trees give logarithmic lookups and keep their keys sorted, and arrays have excellent memory locality; in economic terms, these are simply the going prices of each structure.
cases.notes: Accurate general facts about data-structure costs, but none of what the page teaches (not sophistication but the needed operations, separate representations for different operations, listing the most frequent operations first).
cases.author: F

cases.text: A pattern earns its keep when it renders some recurring design problem easier to understand, and it does so, I would argue, because patterns are the product of a kind of natural selection among designs: only the fittest solutions survive, so whatever has become a pattern is by that very fact already optimised.
credits: makes a recurring design problem easier
cases.notes: The conclusion matches the source (useful when it makes a recurring problem easier to understand), but the 'natural selection has optimised them' reason is unsupported and does not explain understandability; it is not contradicted outright, so no misconception is listed.
cases.author: F

cases.text: Time complexity is a statement about how the amount of work grows as the input gets larger, always relative to some agreed model of what counts as a step: a growth curve, not a stopwatch reading. A linear scan might, in the worst case, have to look at every element; a binary search keeps halving the range still under consideration, but that only works if the data are already arranged in a compatible order, as when one searches an alphabetised herbarium catalogue.
credits: how work grows with input size
linear scan may inspect every element
binary search repeatedly narrows a sorted
the data must have a compatible ordering
cases.notes: Growth relative to a model, the qualified 'may inspect every element', repeated halving and the ordering precondition are all correct.
cases.author: F

cases.text: The page assigns each responsibility an owner: the interface presents state to the user, an application service coordinates the workflow, and persistence commits the durable changes. Handing the screens an immutable summary of the document keeps rendering independent of how things are stored. Codebases that pass a database object through every screen do tend to have boundaries that are hard to change, although I suspect both are simply symptoms of hurried development rather than one causing the other.

misconceptions.claim: makes boundaries difficult to change

credits: The interface presents state
An application service coordinates a workflow
Persistence commits durable changes
immutable document summary keeps rendering separate
cases.notes: The three roles and the benefit of an immutable summary are right, but the final clause turns the source's causal claim (passing a database object through every screen makes boundaries hard to change) into mere co-occurrence with a common cause.
cases.author: F

cases.text: Keys are just row IDs.

cases.text: Here's a rule I give every new developer on day one: never, ever use the array index as a key. Why so strict? Imagine a to-do list keyed by position. The moment you do that, React starts reshuffling things on you — rows jump places, new ones get slotted in where you didn't put them, others vanish. The index key is what sets all that moving around in motion, so just don't.

when items move, are inserted or removed

cases.notes: Turns 'can be a poor key when items move' into 'never', and runs the cause backwards by claiming the index key makes items move, get inserted or vanish, when the source says those changes are what make an index a poor key.

cases.text: An index key is perfectly fine as long as the list never changes shape. So the moment rows get reordered, added or taken out, the index stops being a key you can trust.

misconceptions.claim: dependencies mostly flow inward/ downward

credits: Organize responsibilities into layers
cases.notes: The layers are right, but dependencies are said to run upward from business rules and database to the screens, the reverse of the inward/downward flow, so the spaghetti sentence is not credited either.
cases.author: I

cases.text: An ORM is the translator between our app's world (customers, orders, invoices) and the database, so devs work with those objects instead of writing raw database commands. The reason teams use one is that it makes the database itself answer faster.
credits: maps application objects/models to database operations
cases.notes: The mapping definition is right, but the payoff is pinned on a faster database rather than faster development, parameterized queries and centralized schema access, an unsupported reason rather than a contradicted one.
cases.author: I

cases.text: It lets us ship the code whenever engineering's ready but decide separately when customers actually get the feature: staff first, then 5% of customers, then everyone. So deploy day and launch day aren't glued together anymore, and rollouts get a lot less scary.
credits: enables behavior for selected users/environments
decouples code deployment from feature release
cases.notes: Covers switching behavior on for chosen groups and separating deployment from release for a safer rollout, all in business terms.
cases.author: I

cases.text: Feature flags are basically on/off switches wrapped around a feature, so the code can go out with a normal release but stay hidden until product decides to turn it on, maybe just for internal testers or one region first. That splits 'we deployed it' from 'customers can see it'. And because you can always flip it back off, anything behind a flag is completely risk-free to launch. You do need someone to own each flag and clean it up afterwards, or the old ones pile up.

misconceptions.claim: and supports safer rollout

credits: enables behavior for selected users/environments
cases.notes: Everything is right except the claim that anything behind a flag is completely risk-free, an absolute where the source only says flags support safer rollout, so that sentence is not credited.
cases.author: I

cases.text: Rules the database itself enforces.
credits: A rule enforced by the database
cases.notes: The definition is right, but there is nothing about why (protecting data and invariants even when several parts of the app write), and the purpose is a secondary element, not the core.
cases.author: I

cases.text: Database constraints are really just the access rules, basically authorization done at the database level: which staff can see or change which customer records, like finance can edit invoices but the warehouse team can't. Our app checks those rules first and then tells the database what it's allowed to accept.

misconceptions.claim: such as NOT NULL, CHECK, UNIQUE
A rule enforced by the database

cases.notes: Replaces integrity rules with authorization (who may see or edit records) and has the app enforcing the rules on the database instead of the database enforcing them.
cases.author: I

cases.text: Picture an order-tracking page. While it's fetching, show a placeholder. If the orders come back, show them. If the customer has no orders, say so instead of a blank page. If the call fails, show an error and a retry buton.
credits: loading, success, empty, and error
cases.notes: All four states come through one order-tracking scenario, but the why (networks fail and data can be missing, so production UI must show each state) is never stated; torn with understood, so the less generous label.
cases.author: I

cases.text: A websocket (or webhook, people use both words) is when our system automatically pings the partner's URL the moment an order ships, so they get notified without having to keep checking. It's the only way to do anything real-time, full stop.

misconceptions.claim: A long-lived full-duplex connection
useful when both sides need low-latency

cases.notes: Describes a webhook call to a partner URL instead of a long-lived two-way connection, and calls it the only way to do real-time where the source says it is useful when both sides need low latency.
cases.author: I

cases.text: Kind of like a chat window, new messages just pop up on their own without anyone hitting refresh.
cases.notes: Live chat updates are a correct piece, but there is nothing about a persistent connection over which both client and server send messages.
cases.author: I

cases.text: Two kinds of matching. One asks if they're literally the same one, like the exact same pallet, and the other asks if everything on them matches, box by box, all the way down. Depends which one you use.
cases.notes: Both checks are described, but 'one', 'the other' and 'they' are never tied to reference versus deep equality, so the core mapping is missing and the less generous fragile fits.
cases.author: I

cases.text: TypeScript is JavaScript with a spec sheet bolted on. Before anything runs, it checks that all the pieces match the agreed shapes, so a lot of handoff mistakes between teams get caught early instead of by customers, and the type labels double as documentation of the contract for people and for the editor tools. It can also figure out every single type on its own, so you never actually have to write one.

misconceptions.claim: can often determine a value's type

credits: JavaScript plus a static type system
catches many integration mistakes earlier
cases.notes: Checking before runtime, catching integration mistakes and documenting contracts are right, but 'every single type' and 'never have to write one' overstate the source's 'often'.
cases.author: I

cases.text: TypeScript's the Microsoft one, right? It's everywhere now, half the frontend job posts we put out ask for it.
cases.notes: Who made TypeScript and how popular it is are not what the source teaches, so there is no evidence about static types checked before runtime.
cases.author: I

cases.text: It doesn't mean you can never have two lines that look alike. It's about each business rule, say the discount policy or the shipping-fee formula, living in exactly one place. If that rule gets copied into three spots, sooner or later someone updates two of them, the invoices stop agreeing, and touching that rule again becomes a gamble.
credits: avoid duplicating the same knowledge or rule
Duplicated business rules drift and make maintenance risky
cases.notes: Correctly limits DRY to duplicated rules rather than every repeated line and explains that the copies drift and make changes risky.
cases.author: I

cases.text: Internet basics, pretty much.
cases.notes: Too vague to show whether they know the page is about how browser requests travel, get routed, cached and returned.
cases.author: I
